title: Fleming spotted it. Someone else made it a medicine. Fleming saw the mould killing bacteria in 1928
description:
Fleming saw the mould killing bacteria in 1928. A team in Oxford turned it into a drug. His 1929 paper drew little attention. Florey, Chain and colleagues showed it killed bacteria in living bodies as well as in dishes.

Oxford police officer and the first patient given penicillin, on 12 February 1941. He improved, then the supply ran out and he died.

The mould grew as a thin film, so output stayed tiny. Corn steep liquor, a cheap corn belt by-product, and a better strain found on a mouldy fruit in a Peoria market made large scale production possible.

2.3 million doses had been made in time for the Normandy landings. Allied soldiers carried the antibiotic onto the beaches on 6 June 1944.

Units of penicillin a year being made in the United States by June 1945.

One mould. Three Nobel winners.

Sources:

Established Fleming's observation on 3 September 1928 and publication in 1929, that he did not convince anyone it was important because it was so difficult to isolate, that Florey, Chain and colleagues at Oxford concentrated it and showed bactericidal action in vitro and in vivo, that policeman Albert Alexander was treated in 1941, improved, and died when the supply ran out, that the 1945 Nobel Prize was shared by Chain, Fleming and Florey, that 2.3 million doses were made in time for the Normandy invasion, and that over 646 billion units a year were being made by June 1945.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Fleming: read in full. Established that the 1945 prize citation was for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases, that the 1929 paper drew little attention, and that the popular claim that Fleming abandoned penicillin in the early 1930s is disputed.
- https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1945/summary/: read. Confirmed the 1945 prize in Physiology or Medicine went jointly to Fleming, Chain and Florey, with the motivation 'for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases'.
- https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/how-world-war-ii-put-penicillin-into-every-pharmacy: read in full. Established that Florey's team turned penicillin from a laboratory curiosity into a practical antibiotic, that Albert Alexander received the first dose on 12 February 1941, that the mould grew only as a thin film, that corn steep liquor and a strain from a rotten melon in a Peoria market solved production, and that 2.3 million doses were made for D-Day.
